title: Independent contractor vs employee: How to tell the difference
summary: Know where contractor vs employee status really differs. Compare control, tax, benefits and the IRS classification tests in one place. Get the breakdown.
body_markdown:
A new job offer can feel straightforward until you reach the part of the contract that describes your employment status. The salary may look attractive and the role may seem like the right next step, but being hired as an independent contractor rather than an employee can change what you take home, who handles your taxes and whether you receive benefits such as paid leave or health insurance.


An independent contractor runs their own business and controls how they work, while an employee works under the employer's direction. Employers withhold tax and provide benefits for employees, but not for contractors, who handle their own taxes


The difference is more than a job title, and getting it wrong can leave you with unexpected tax bills or fewer workplace protections than you expected. In this guide, we’ll break down the key differences between an independent contractor and an employee, so you can understand where you stand before signing your next contract.


## **Independent contractor vs employee: Key differences**


This table compares the main differences between contractors and employees, from workplace control and taxes to benefits, job security, tools, and financial risk.


Feature Independent Contractor Employee


Control Dictates own hours, methods, and routine Employer dictates schedule, location, and tasks


Tax Pays own income and self-employment taxes Employer automatically withholds income and payroll taxes


Benefits Responsible for own health insurance and retirement Eligible for company healthcare, 401(k), and PTO


Tools Provides own specialised equipment and software Employer provides necessary tools and equipment


Permanence Defined by project completion or contract end Indefinite, ongoing relationship until termination


Financial Risk Can experience a financial profit or loss Receives a guaranteed wage or salary

## **What is an independent contractor?**


An independent contractor is a self-employed person who provides services to a business or individual under a contract rather than working as a traditional employee. Think of a freelance designer hired to create a company’s new website, a consultant brought in to solve a business problem, or a writer paid to produce a series of articles. They work independently and are generally responsible for deciding how, when, and where the work gets done, as long as they deliver what was agreed in the contract.


In the US, independent contractors are commonly paid as 1099 workers, meaning businesses generally report their payments to the contractor using a[Form 1099-NEC](https://grey.co/blog/what-is-a-1099) when applicable. Unlike employees, contractors typically do not have income tax, Social Security, or Medicare taxes withheld from their payments, so they need to plan for these taxes themselves.


Being an independent contractor also comes with responsibilities beyond completing the work. Contractors usually handle their own tax filings, business expenses, insurance and retirement planning, while keeping records of income and expenses. The trade-off is greater control over how they work and, in many cases, the ability to work with multiple clients.


## **What is an Employee?**


An employee is a person who works for a company or organisation under an employment relationship, where the employer generally controls what work is done, how it is performed and when it is completed. Unlike an independent contractor, an employee works as part of the organisation and is typically entitled to protections and benefits provided under their employment arrangement.


### **W-2 Pay**


In the US, employees are generally paid through payroll and receive a W-2 form from their employer at the end of the tax year. The W-2 reports their wages and the taxes already withheld from their pay.


### **Tax Withholding**


Employers typically withhold federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare taxes from an employee’s wages and send these amounts to the relevant authorities. This means employees do not usually need to set aside the full tax amount themselves.


### **Employee Benefits**


Depending on the employer and role, employees may receive health insurance, retirement plans, paid time off and other benefits. If you encounter the term “[what a 1099 employee is](https://grey.co/blog/what-is-a-1099-employee) ,” it is important to understand that a 1099 worker is generally an independent contractor, not an employee.


## **How the IRS tests classification**


The difference between an employee and an independent contractor is not always obvious from a job title or contract. A company might call someone a contractor, but the IRS looks at the actual working relationship to determine how that person should be classified for tax purposes. It generally considers three categories of control.


### **Behavioral Control**


The IRS considers whether the business has the right to direct how, when and where the worker performs their job. Detailed instructions, set working hours, training and supervision can indicate an employee relationship.


### **Financial Control**


The IRS looks at how much control the business has over the worker’s financial and business activities. Factors include who provides tools and equipment, whether expenses are reimbursed, how the worker is paid and whether they can make a profit or experience a loss.


### **Relationship Factors**


The nature of the relationship also matters, including written contracts, employee benefits, how permanent the arrangement is and whether the worker provides services that are a key part of the business. No single factor determines classification; the IRS considers the entire relationship.


### **How taxes and paperwork differ for Contractors and Employees**


Getting paid as a contractor or employee does not just change the amount that lands in your bank account; it also changes the paperwork you receive, who handles your tax withholding and what happens if your worker classification is wrong.


### **1099 vs. W-2**


Employees generally receive a W-2 showing their wages and taxes withheld by their employer, while independent contractors typically receive a 1099-NEC for qualifying payments.[Understanding 1099 vs. W-2](https://grey.co/blog/1099-vs-w2) can help clarify how each worker is paid, what taxes are withheld, who is responsible for reporting income, and what paperwork to expect.


### **Self-Employment Tax**


Contractors generally have to account for both the employer and employee portions of Social Security and Medicare taxes through[self-employment tax](https://grey.co/blog/freelancer-vs-employee-tax) , meaning they need to plan for these payments themselves rather than relying on payroll withholding.


### **Misclassification risk**


Calling a worker a contractor does not automatically make them one. If a business treats an employee as an independent contractor, it may face additional taxes, penalties and other consequences, while the worker could miss protections and benefits they should have received.

## **Frequently asked questions**


### **What is the difference between a contractor and an employee?**


An employee works under an employer’s direction and typically receives payroll withholding and benefits, while an independent contractor runs their own business and controls how they complete their work. Contractors generally handle their own taxes, business expenses and insurance, while employees receive greater workplace protections and employer-provided benefits.


### **How does the IRS decide?**


The IRS looks beyond a worker’s job title or contract and examines the actual working relationship. It considers behavioural control, financial control and the relationship between the worker and business. No single factor automatically determines classification, so businesses should consider the full arrangement when deciding whether someone is an employee or contractor.


### **Do contractors get benefits?**


Independent contractors generally do not receive employee benefits such as employer-sponsored health insurance, paid vacation or retirement contributions. Instead, they are responsible for arranging their own insurance, retirement savings and other benefits. However, a contractor’s specific agreement can provide certain perks or payments, depending on what the business and contractor negotiate.


### **What is misclassification?**


Misclassification happens when a business treats a worker as an independent contractor when the person legally qualifies as an employee. This can affect taxes, benefits and workplace protections. For the business, misclassification can lead to unpaid employment taxes, penalties and other costs, while the worker may lose benefits they should have received.


### **Can someone be both?**


Yes, someone can potentially work as an employee for one business while independently contracting for another. For example, a person could have a full-time W-2 job and provide freelance consulting services to separate clients. However, the classification of each working relationship depends on the specific facts and circumstances involved.


### **How do I pay an overseas contractor?**


Paying an overseas contractor typically involves choosing a payment method, confirming the contractor’s banking details and considering currency conversion, transfer fees and tax documentation.
